balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Aflac Incorporated: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Aflac Incorporated: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Aflac Incorporated: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Aflac Incorporated: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Aflac Incorporated: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Aflac Incorporated: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Aflac Incorporated: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

persistency.title: Premium persistency
persistency.content:
Persistency is the percentage of annualized premium in force a year earlier that is still in force today -- the inverse of the lapse rate.

For Aflac Incorporated: Japan persistency in the low-to-mid 90s reflects decades-old, mostly paid-up third-sector policies; U.S. persistency runs structurally lower (high 70s) because voluntary/supplemental products sold through employers turn over with jobs. The two are not comparable levels, only comparable trends.

What to watch:

  • A declining trend in either market, which erodes the in-force base faster than new sales can replace it
  • Japan persistency falling meaningfully below its historical band -- the back book is the bulk of segment profit

premiumsInForce.title: Annualized premiums in force
premiumsInForce.content:
Annualized premiums in force is the annualized premium on all policies currently active -- the stock of the business, versus new sales which is the flow.

For Aflac Incorporated: Japan is disclosed in ¥ (here scaled to ¥bn) and U.S. in $bn -- a roughly 170x difference in units, not in the relative size of the two books once converted to a common currency. Plot each against its own axis; never compare the raw numbers.

What to watch:

  • Japan's in-force base shrinking as the legacy block runs off faster than new Japan sales replace it
  • U.S. in-force growing in line with the new-sales trend above

premiumsInForceGrowth.title: Annualized premiums in force -- YoY growth
premiumsInForceGrowth.content:
Year-over-year growth in annualized premiums in force for each segment, independent of currency -- this is the number to compare Japan against U.S. directly, unlike the levels chart above.

For Aflac Incorporated: Japan has run negative for years (a shrinking, mostly paid-up back book); U.S. has run positive. The net of the two is the thesis on whether U.S. growth is big enough to offset Japan's runoff.

What to watch:

  • Japan's rate of decline steepening or stabilizing
  • U.S. growth decelerating, which would leave the combined in-force book shrinking

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Aflac Incorporated: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Aflac Incorporated: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Aflac Incorporated: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
